title: arXiv AI daily — 29 October 2026
global_caveat: arXiv has no official trending chart; this is an inferred ordering, not a readership ranking. These papers are very recent, and Semantic Scholar currently reports zero citations for each selected paper.

sections.title: Prefix Executability: Evaluating Tool-Using Agents Beyond Final Success
sections.abstract: The authors propose measuring whether every intermediate tool-call prefix remains executable, and report that final-success rankings can conceal invalid trajectories.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors define Prefix Executability Curves and related measures, evaluate on BFCL-v3, ToolSandbox, and τ³-bench, and report that explicit pre-execution plan checking can improve executable-prefix survival.
sections.unique_caveat: Evaluation covers stratified samples from BFCL-v3 and ToolSandbox and the Airline/Retail base splits of τ³-bench, rather than every tool-use setting.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The arXiv record says the paper was accepted to NeurIPS 2026 and it is cross-listed in two core AI categories; its trajectory-level reliability measures make it a concrete evaluation contribution.

sections.title: Gym-Anything for Robotics: Scaling physical simulations with digital agents
sections.abstract: The authors use coding agents and an adversarial creation-audit loop to build RoboWorld, a 25-simulation robotics benchmark, and report that frontier-model performance improves with several simulation-based learning methods.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors construct 25 simulations with 25 test and 175 training RL environments; they report that the best frontier models average 0.06 reward on RoboWorld test tasks and that privileged-state learning methods improve results.
sections.unique_caveat: The reported evaluation is in simulation; the paper does not establish transfer from RoboWorld to physical robots.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Cross-listed across three core AI categories; the paper releases its simulation pipeline, environments, and benchmark, with a companion project page and code repository.

sections.title: VeriCUA: Verification as Agentic Exploration for Computer-Using Agents
sections.abstract: VeriCUA treats computer-agent verification as active evidence gathering, combining GUI and code checks to assess unresolved task requirements across platforms and settings.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors introduce a platform-agnostic verifier that builds a task rubric, selects GUI or code checks for unmet requirements, and combines findings under explicit evidence rules; they report better agreement than compared baselines.
sections.unique_caveat: The arXiv record labels the work Work in progress, and the reported results concern the evaluated computer-use settings rather than all agent environments.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: Cross-listed across three core AI categories, and the paper reports comparisons across online/offline settings, platforms, and observation modalities.

sections.title: Retrieval as Traversal: Value-Indexed Memory for Stateful Long-Context Agents
sections.abstract: The paper proposes persistent local traversal over a value-indexed memory address space and reports a proof-of-principle result on MiniGrid Memory using a five-token context.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors separate memory content from its address and optimize local access for complementary rather than redundant information; on MiniGrid Memory they report 0.95 mean return after 0.59M steps with a five-token context.
sections.unique_caveat: The paper tests only a fixed-geometry proof of principle; it does not test learned geometry or repeated retrieval and explicitly calls for further experiments.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The arXiv record lists acceptance at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Long-Context Foundation Models; its experiment offers a concrete, checkable test of a persistent-retrieval approach.

sections.title: FARMS: A Verifiable Foundation for Automated Computational Science
sections.abstract: FARMS links mathematical statements to source context, algorithms, and guarantees, then connects selected statements through Lean-checked implications to scientific-computing skills.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors report 157 pipeline-accepted formalizations across 171 targets and illustrate reuse in a heat-flow solve and wave-response compression with stated error guarantees.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors’ collection covers four sources in two areas of computational mathematics, and the numerical demonstrations are limited to two applications; broader source coverage and application checks remain open.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The paper is cross-listed into logic and provides a public code repository and project page; its 171-target study and two numerical applications provide a measurable evaluation footprint.

sections.title: Training Foundation Models with a Single Algorithm
sections.abstract: The authors formulate pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and suitable reinforcement-learning updates as likelihood fitting over evolving mixtures of static data and model-generated examples.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors present a common maximum-likelihood trainer for static and generated data and report improvements in accuracy-compute tradeoff and task coverage in their evaluated settings.
sections.unique_caveat: The authors describe the experiments as small-scale, note that most runs optimize one RL task at a time, and leave predictive scaling laws and a universally preferred data mixture unresolved.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The paper supplies a public project website, code, and model/data resources and reports both controlled and real-world experiments; it has one core-category listing.

sections.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
sections.abstract: The authors introduce rewindable interactive proofs, in which a verifier can restore an AI prover’s prior state, and construct an oversight protocol for computations robust to a small fraction of changed oracle answers.
sections.claimed_contribution: The authors construct a relativizing rewindable proof for computations robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers and report a preliminary MNIST implementation that is faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system.
sections.unique_caveat: The construction applies to the stated robustness class and depends on the verifier being able to checkpoint and restore the prover; the empirical demonstration is preliminary and on MNIST.
sections.evidence_for_ranking: The work spans AI, computational complexity, and security, presents an explicit efficiency analysis, and links an implementation; empirical evidence is preliminary.
